heading: Seed and seed control
body: Seed is the place the next season starts from.
When your household can save, keep and share good seed, it carries more than a harvest. It also carries the freedom to choose.
In this lesson you will follow seed from the parent plant to the packet, to the germination test and to the neighbour's hand.
Think about the crops of your place. Which ones do you save seed of now? Which seed do you buy? Which seed do you swap?
Try to describe at least one crop whose seed is already being saved in your place.

heading: Why saving seed matters
body: Saving seed does not mean rejecting all bought seed. It means building a working choice.
Each crop that you learn to save well removes some repeated buying. It starts with a local record of what works well in your soil and in your season.
Think about the seed you buy again and again. Which repeated seed-buying costs your household the most in a year?
Choose one crop from your planting list. Make it your first working place of seed saving. Do not try to save everything at one time.

heading: Learning outcomes
body: This lesson ends in a working seed store, not in a list of facts.
You will make four decisions.
What will you save?
How will you prepare it?
How will you protect it?
And how will you know it is still alive before you rely on it?
Which of these four decisions is the most unusual for you?
Say them again in your own words: choose, prepare, protect and confirm.

heading: Open-pollinated and F1 seed
body: There is no magic/charm in open-pollinated seed.
A stable variety can produce similar generations when it is separated properly or pollinates itself.
F1 seed stays alive. But the next generation splits into different combinations of the parents' traits.
The problem is unpredictability, not failure to germinate.
Think of one small bed in your place. Why can unexpected plants be a danger when the place is small?
If you have seed packets, look whether they are marked open-pollinated or F1. Which one can you choose in order to save seed that can be trusted?
Remember: the next F1 generation is different. It does not die by itself.

heading: Watch: open-pollinated and F1 seed
body: Watch both sides.
Both kinds of seed germinate.
Open-pollinated seed produces similar plants when the variety is stable and pollination is controlled properly.
Seed saved from an F1 plant also germinates. But its next generation is different. Some plants may be tall. Others short. Their vigour and harvest may differ.
Ask yourself what this means when you choose seed that will be saved.
If you understand the difference, you can explain it in one sentence: both germinate, but the next F1 generation is not predictable.

heading: Seed control
body: Seed control is not seen in a slogan.
It is seen in a dry packet, in a written record and in knowing how the seed behaves.
Your household starts it. Neighbours extend it. The seasons of the year make a local seed collection more useful.
Which seed does your household already save best?
Draw a small map of households near you. Next to each household write one crop that household can help with in seed exchange.
Control needs three things: usable seed, written information and exchange.

heading: Watch: household seed network
body: Well-saved seed becomes stronger when it is known and shared.
Watch one household start by saving the seed of one crop well. Dry seed goes into clean packets. Some packets go to nearby households. Neighbours share different seed in return.
In the end each household holds more varieties than before.
Think about seed you can share and seed you can receive from neighbours. Seed travels. Knowledge and trust must travel with it.

heading: Choose many parent plants
body: The biggest fruit is not always a good seed parent.
Look at the whole plant.
Was it healthy?
Did it ripen at the right time?
Was it like its type?
Save from many good plants, especially cross-pollinated plants. This prevents the next generation from coming from only one parent.
What can you do about this seed plant even if its fruit is big? (garbled)
Go to your place. Point out plants you could choose and ones you could breed from. Choose many healthy plants that are like their type. Reject plants with disease and ones not like their type.

heading: Control pollination
body: Some plants mostly pollinate themselves. So a small garden can keep the variety the same.
Plants that are given pollen by wind or are with insects can mix over a long distance.
The needed distance depends on the plant, the place and the purpose of the seed. Do not promise purity of variety until you have tested the plant.
How can you separate two varieties without using distance?
You can plant them at different times so they don't flower together. You can control pollination by hand or use covers.
Remember three tools: distance, flowering time or controlled pollination.

heading: Watch: self-pollination and crossing
body: Follow the way pollen travels.
In self-pollination, pollen moves inside one flower from the part that produces it to the part that receives it. This usually helps the variety stay the same.

In a maize field, wind carries pollen from the tassels (flowers at the head of the maize) to the silks (threads coming out of the cob). If two varieties are near and flower at the same time, they can mix.
Think how distance or different flowering times could prevent that in your place.

heading: Dry and wet processing
body: There are two big ways of processing seed.
Dry seed ripens in the pod, in the head or on the cob. It is gathered when fully ripe.
Seed in a fleshy fruit must first be separated from the flesh.
Short fermentation is useful especially for tomato seed. It is not a rule for all plants with wet seeds.
Think of crops of your place. Which suit the dry way? Which suit the wet way?
If you have seeds or fruit nearby, sort them into these two kinds. Explain the difference by describing what the seed is like at harvest time.

heading: Process dry seed
body: Leave plants with dry seeds on the plant until the seed is fully ripe.
Gather it before weather, birds or bursting pods take the harvest.
Remove chaff and damaged seed.
Then spread clean seed in one layer in moving air and in shade.
What tells you that dry seed is ripe enough to be gathered?
If you have a dry pod or seed head, hold it. Listen to the seed. Compare something green and soft with something brown and cracking.
Wait for ripeness. For final drying, use shade and moving air.

heading: Watch: dry processing
body: Let the seed ripen on the plant before gathering it.
Watch how it is gathered when it is ripe. Chaff and rubbish are removed. Damaged seed is thrown out.
Clean seed is spread in one layer in moving air and in shade.
Follow the steps in order: ripen, gather, clean, dry.
Think where you can do each part of this process.

heading: Wet processing of tomato seed
body: Take out the tomato seed with its flesh and put it in a clean jar with a little water.
Leave it open or loosely covered. Keep it out of strong sun.
After two to three days, there may be a light film and a sour smell.
Rinse quickly. Remove rubbish. Then spread clean seed thinly to dry.
Do not close a jar that is still fermenting.
Think about signs that tell you the process has started. Think also about signs that would make you throw away the batch.
Get a jar, a sieve and a drying plate. When ready, start a small batch. Remember the order: take out, ferment a short time, rinse and then dry completely.

heading: Watch: wet processing of tomato seed
body: Watch the whole process in order.
A ripe tomato is opened. Seed and jelly are poured into a clean jar. Only a little water is added.
The jar is left open or loosely covered for two to three days.
When a light film and a sour smell appear, the middle is poured onto a sieve. The seed is rinsed until clean.
At the end, the seed is spread in one layer in shade until completely dry.
Repeat the steps to yourself: take out, ferment a short time, rinse, dry completely.

heading: Practical task
body: Here the lesson leaves the screen and arrives in your hands.
Start one batch of seed processed wet.
Use one ripe and healthy fruit, a clean jar, a spoon, a little water, a sieve and a drying plate.
Put seed, flesh and a little water in the jar. Stick on a dated label.
You will look after this jar after the lesson. Decide now when you will check it, when you will rinse it and when you will dry the seed.
Your jar needs a date and a plan for coming back. Write down the date you will check it after two days.

heading: Dry first, close later
body: Drying is not a decorative final step.
Wet seed keeps breathing. It can heat up, rot or die in storage.
Use shade, moving air and time.
Close the seed only when you are sure it is dry.
Which place in your home has shade and air but is safe from rain and cooking steam?
Choose one safe drying place. Then identify one place that is not safe.
Repeat this to check your understanding: dry first, close later.

heading: Protect seed from heat, light and damp
body: Paper packets breathe and organise seed. But they are not enough in damp weather.
Once the seed is completely dry, put the named packets inside a closed container that protects from damp. If you have it, include a food-safe desiccant (thing that holds moisture).
Keep the container as cool and dark as possible in your home.
Which room or cupboard in your home stays cool and very dry?
Compare a paper envelope alone with an envelope inside a closed container.
Safe storage has two levels: a named paper packet inside a dry, closed container.

heading: Label every packet
body: Storage protects the seed physically. Written information protects its meaning.
A packet must tell the next person which crop it is.
It must give the variety name or local name.
It must say when the seed was saved and where it comes from.
Which local names could be lost if you write only the crop name?
Take an empty packet. Practise writing four pieces of information: crop, variety or local name, date and source.
Check again that all four are there.

heading: Ten-seed germination test
body: A seed packet can look perfect even if the seed is losing life.
Ten seeds make counting easy.
Keep them warm and wet. Do not drown them in water.
Then count the small plants that have grown normally.
Six out of ten is about sixty percent. That tells you to plant more densely, use the seed as a test only, or replace it.
If eight out of ten seeds germinate, how many percent is that?
The answer is eighty percent.
Start a ten-seed test using an old packet. Write down the date and the day on which you will count.

heading: Watch: ten-seed germination test
body: Count exactly ten seeds.
Put them in two rows of five seeds.
Keep them on paper or wet cloth. Do not drown them in water.
After some time, count again.
Here, six have germinated. Four have not germinated. The total stays ten.
So the germination rate is sixty percent.
Test yourself. Did you count ten at the start, six seeds that germinated and four seeds that did not germinate at the end?

heading: Share seed and its information
body: Exchanging seed is not a table of unknown packets.
Good exchange moves information along with the seed.
It tells what the seed is. Where it comes from. When it was saved. And whether it has been tested.
This honesty will strengthen the whole network.
What information could help you trust seed from another household?
Take one of your packets. Practise describing it before sharing. Give the seed together with its basic history.

heading: Field task
body: This task is small enough to be finished. But it is very important.
Build one working container for storing seed.
Put named paper packets inside a dry, closed container.
Take a photo of it.
Then describe the crop whose seed you will save this season.
The photo is evidence. The packet is the first thing.
What have you not yet found in order to finish this at home?
Write a short list of supplies. Choose a date to finish.
Before closing the container, check your work: seed completely dry; each packet has crop, variety and date; container cool, dark and safe from damp; and you chose many healthy parent plants.

heading: Field action
body: Choose.
Prepare.
Protect.
Confirm.
Those four actions carry the seed collection from this field to the next season.
Start with one crop and do it well.
Which crop will you start with?
Say its name out loud. Then choose one action you will do next.
The next season is already in the seed you choose today.
